title: A season (Ecclesiastes 3:1–8)
hook: "To every thing there is a season"

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kohelet's opening cry: hevel, breath of breaths. Your line was nothing stays in the hand. Today, the same book turns its breath into a rhythm, and the week comes to a close.

Same afternoon, same street. On one porch, a family is setting out chairs for a party, balloons tied to the railing. Three doors down, the curtains are drawn, and cars line the curb at a house of mourning. A man walks past both houses on the way to buy milk. Nobody on that street is doing life wrong. They're just in different hours of it. Kohelet has a poem for that street. It reads like a list, and it works like a clock.
screen: `A PARTY ON ONE PORCH.` → `MOURNING THREE DOORS DOWN.` → `DIFFERENT HOURS OF ONE LIFE.`

segments.voice: Ecclesiastes chapter three, in the King James words: "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven: A time to be born, and a time to die." A time to plant, and a time to pluck up. A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance. A time to keep silence, and a time to speak. And at the end: a time to love, and a time to hate; a time of war, and a time of peace. Every line holds two opposites side by side, and neither cancels the other. The poem doesn't say mourning is bad and dancing is good. Each has its hour. Yesterday, Kohelet called everything breath. Today he hints at something steadier underneath: a little further on, he says God hath made every thing beautiful in his time. Not every moment is beautiful on its own, but each one has a place. Readers take the poem two ways. Some find comfort: grief won't last forever, and neither will this hard stretch. Others hear a challenge: you don't choose the season, but you can ask what this one is for. A time to speak, or to keep silence? To plant, or to wait? The poem doesn't answer for you. It just insists the question is real.
screen: `TO EVERY THING THERE IS A SEASON.` · `PAIRS OF OPPOSITES, SIDE BY SIDE.` · then, large: `EVERY THING BEAUTIFUL IN HIS TIME.` · then: `WHAT IS THIS SEASON FOR?`

segments.voice: This week ran from Mishlei and the first step through the door, through atzei chayim, rakh, each child's own way and bread for an enemy, to breath that can't be held. Now let a pair from the poem find you, plant or pluck up, weep or laugh, keep silence or speak, and notice not the one you wish for but the one that's true. Say quietly, this is a time to, and finish the line; if you pray, you can bring that season with you into prayer.
A season. Ecclesiastes three: to every thing there is a season, pairs of opposites, each with its own hour. Today's word.
Your line: a time for everything. Each hour has its place, the hard ones too. That's day eight hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: Ecclesiastes 3 belongs to Kohelet, one of the five scrolls of the Writings, and some Jews quote its 'a time to' lines at turning points in life, from celebrations to houses of mourning.

chat.says: Is 'a time to every purpose' saying some times of life are good and others bad?
options: No. Each line pairs opposites, and the poem gives each its own hour, without ranking.
Yes. It lists the happy times first, so you'll know which ones to choose.
Yes. The poem says to hurry past the sad times to reach the happy ones.
chat.meaning: Ecclesiastes 3 pairs opposites, weeping and laughing, mourning and dancing, and gives each its hour: God hath made every thing beautiful in his time.
